status: DISMISSED — demurrer to FAC sustained without leave to amend July 15, 2026 (Hon. George J. Abdallah, Jr.) on exhaustion grounds. $85,000 global demand rejected May 23, 2026. Dismissal supplies predicate facts for Matter 28 (NDCA HOPE complaint).
key_facts: Matter 5 (FAC filed April 22, 2026) asserts seven state causes of action against HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. and its Stockton site Director Katie Palacios (LMFT No. 44555, CASOMB-certified), sued individually and as a managing agent of HOPE under Civil Code §3294(b). The FAC drops False Imprisonment (original complaint) and adds Negligence Per Se, Declaratory Relief, and UCL §17200. The central theory is institutional fraud: HOPE represented at intake (March 5, 2021) — through materials, treatment contract, and verbal orientation — that it offered an individualized, achievable path to treatment completion, while concealing its blanket retention policy under which no parolee can ever complete treatment prior to parole discharge, regardless of clinical progress, compliance, or risk score. HOPE's own Executive Director of Clinical Training, Dr. Cristina Loree, admitted this policy under oath in In re Dwyer, No. SC-080355A (San Mateo County Super. Ct., Mar. 20, 2023) (Hill, J.), and the court found the policy 'vitiates the Legislature's directive' under Penal Code §3008(d)(2). HOPE continued applying the identical policy after Dwyer and after the April 17, 2025 effective date of 15 CCR §3574(f)(1), which requires treatment completion and parole discharge to be legally separate decisions. Financial incentive: each retained parolee generates ~$10,600/year in baseline group and CTM revenue; no fee for completion; discharge terminates the revenue. Key fraud incidents: (1) Clinician Pamela Akins, November 2022 group session: represented HOPE applied objective individualized criteria and Plaintiff had a meaningful path to completion; (2) January 2024 group session (clinician under Palacios's supervision): stated 'individuals are titrating and completing the HOPE program'; (3) June 2024 individual session: Palacios, through a clinician, falsely stated that no homework completed by Plaintiff had ever been found in HOPE's records — false, as Palacios herself admitted in an August 2025 video-recorded group session that HOPE routinely loses client homework packets; (4) CTM submissions via CDCR Form 3043 at each semi-annual CTM (February and August cycles, 2021–February 2026): Palacios submitted reports to Plaintiff's parole agents (Magana, Arestad, Acierto, Urrea, Long Moua #7472) and supervising agent Noguchi (#7284) characterizing Plaintiff as having 'partially completed homework packets,' 'partial participation,' 'not completed' treatment — all false, predetermined policy outputs rather than individualized clinical assessments. CDCR reliance: five separate parole agents each stated to Plaintiff in substance that 'HOPE controls — without sex-offender completion there will be no discharge from parole.' November 2025 Form 1502-DR incorporated HOPE's non-completion recommendation as the treatment-based predicate for 'Discharge Denied/No Action.' August 2025 CTM (retaliatory statements, Bane Act): Palacios stated in front of Agent Chow, Noguchi (#7284), and Derrick (#6910) that Plaintiff was 'disruptive during HOPE group sessions,' a 'ringleader,' his behavior 'abhorrent,' 'often disrespectful to [her] staff,' and characterized his polite demeanor at the CTM as an 'acting job'; added 'because when you start complaining then the other guys chime in.' FAC alleges these were retaliatory and defamatory, made to intimidate Plaintiff from complaining about treatment conditions. Economic harm: $32,447 lost in 2022 + $60,855 in 2023 + $16,106 in 2024 = $109,408 for 2022–2024, with continuing losses at ~$6,000/month, caused by mandatory HOPE attendance (GPS, curfew, geographic restrictions) incompatible with CDL long-haul work. Plaintiff forced to resign from United Road in January 2022; turned down dispatches for Keurig Dr Pepper, Tiger Lines LLC, US-1 Shorthaul, Lazer Spot Inc., and Centerline Drivers. Special relationship theory: HOPE was sole CASOMB-certified provider in Stockton region; CDCR delegated to HOPE exclusive authority over treatment-status determinations; HOPE knew its representations would be acted upon by CDCR; establishing duty of care under Giraldo v. Cal. Dep't of Corrections & Rehabilitation (2008) 168 Cal.App.4th 231. Discovery rule tolling: Plaintiff did not discover impossibility of completion until reviewing the Dwyer order in late 2025 — Dwyer was a San Mateo County habeas decision never provided to Plaintiff by HOPE or CDCR.
procedural_status: Complaint filed Feb. 10, 2026; FAC filed Apr. 22, 2026 (STK-CV-UF-2026-0001032). Demurrer briefed May–July 2026; hearing July 15, 2026. Court confirmed its tentative and granted the demurrer WOLA for failure to exhaust administrative remedies — disposing the state action. June 8 discovery (RFA responses + RFP production) supplied admissions and documentary support for the blanket-retention / CTM theories later carried into Matter 28; underlying production PDFs were removed from the public repository after review. $85,000 global settlement demand (Matters 3/5/6) rejected by SLB May 23, 2026. Detailed Bates findings and dated briefing beats live in timeline.json / Matter 28 risk.
damages: Compensatory: $109,408 documented CDL wage loss for 2022–2024 ($32,447 in 2022 + $60,855 in 2023 + $16,106 in 2024) plus ~$6,000/month continuing; costs of compliance with unlawful supervision conditions; non-economic damages for emotional distress, humiliation, anxiety, sleep disruption, and loss of liberty. Statutory: Civil Code §52.1 ($25,000 per Bane Act violation). Punitive: Civil Code §3294 — Palacios sued as managing agent enabling entity-level punitive damages against HOPE; conduct continued post-Dwyer (March 2023) and post-§3574 (April 2025). UCL restitution of all fees wrongfully retained by HOPE. Attorney's fees (Civ. Code §52.1(i); CCP §1021.5). Prejudgment and postjudgment interest.
risk: CRITICAL — July 13, 2026 tentative ruling threatens to end this case entirely: the court tentatively agrees with Defendants that failure to exhaust administrative remedies is a jurisdictional bar to the FAC and would GRANT the Demurrer WITHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND, which — if confirmed at the July 15 hearing — terminates all seven causes of action with no ability to replead. This is a tentative ruling only; Plaintiff has filed a timely notice of intent to appear and argue, and Plaintiff's strongest counter-argument (that exhaustion doctrine, designed for writs challenging administrative/parole decisions, does not apply to a private damages action against non-state-actor defendants HOPE/Palacios, reinforced by 15 CCR §3574(e)'s express separation of treatment-completion review from discharge decisions) was not addressed in the tentative's one-paragraph reasoning — a live opening for oral argument. If the tentative is confirmed, Plaintiff's fallback request for leave to amend becomes the only remaining avenue, and even that was denied in the tentative as posted. Below reflects the risk profile as it stood before this ruling; all of it is now contingent on surviving July 15. Markedly favorable risk profile: neither HOPE nor Palacios can invoke qualified immunity or sovereign immunity — both are private contractors. FAC strengthens the case on multiple axes: (1) Palacios sued as managing agent under §3294(b) enables corporate punitive damages against HOPE without requiring officer-level authorization separately; (2) Negligence Per Se under PC §3008(d)(2) and 15 CCR §3574(f)(1) shifts burden on breach element; (3) UCL §17200 claim adds restitution and injunctive relief with potential class-action reach for similarly situated parolees; (4) Declaratory Relief and permanent injunction provide equitable remedy independent of damages; (5) Discovery rule tolling addresses any limitations challenge — Dwyer was inaccessible to Plaintiff until late 2025. The August 2025 video-recorded admission by Palacios that HOPE routinely loses homework packets is near-dispositive on fraud scienter. HOPE's own Executive Director's sworn testimony in Dwyer establishes corporate knowledge of the unlawful policy from March 2023 forward. Continued application after Dwyer and after April 2025 regulatory amendments supports exemplary damages under §3294. HOPE is also exposed to state-actor liability under West v. Atkins in parallel federal Matter 6. Favorable findings in Matters 3, 5, or 6 create compounding collateral estoppel pressure across all proceedings. July 2026 document production materially advances and complicates the case. HOPE's own Clinical Operational Manual verbatim confirms the disputed 'Aftercare Phase' language tying continued treatment to the full term of community supervision, and separately defines a parole-term-expiration 'Discharge' distinct from clinical 'graduation' — direct documentary support undercutting any defense argument that completion was always individually achievable. HOPE's own records also show a no-show logged despite an acknowledged 'technological error,' and no formal 'partially completed' status category exists anywhere in HOPE's own tracking taxonomy, undermining the accuracy of HOPE's CTM reporting to CDCR. Countervailing considerations: HOPE's internal March 2026 homework audit shows genuine, unresolved completion gaps (not merely lost paperwork) in the Preparatory phase and Block 2 of the Core Program, which the defense will likely argue shows non-completion was substantively real rather than fabricated; a Feb. 20, 2025 collateral note timestamps the grace-period revocation roughly two months earlier than pled in the FAC, a discrepancy that should be reconciled; and an October 2023 third-party polygraph note records a 'significant response' to sensitive questions (which Plaintiff denied) that the defense may attempt to use, though it predates the retaliation-period allegations by nearly two years and is inconclusive on its face. The Preparatory Treatment Manual and Employee Handbook show HOPE does use objective, countable completion criteria for the initial Prep phase (≤2 excused absences, completed homework, presented assignments) — narrowing the 'wholly subjective system' characterization to the Maintenance/Core phases specifically, where graduation criteria remain genuinely undefined and team/CD-discretion-based. No document produced to date supports the ~$10,600/year per-client revenue figure or any CDCR billing/incentive structure — that evidence, if it exists, has not yet been produced and should be a discovery-compulsion target.
